title: South Korea to Survey Young K-Pop Stars on Rights
paragraphs: K-pop has become one of South Korea's most successful cultural exports, with groups like BTS, Blackpink, Stray Kids and Babymonster finding fans around the world.
Their slick choreography and highly polished performances are hard work, though. Would-be stars have to do intense training, often starting at a young age.
The South Korean government has now announced plans to survey underage performers on their contracts after a New York Times report prompted concerns over the rights of young K-pop stars.

South Korea's Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism plans to do the survey in 2027, with the goal of examining whether existing rules do enough to protect underage performers' rights to education and rest.
It aims to find out exactly how many underage artists are currently represented by entertainment agencies in South Korea, their ages, and if their basic rights are being respected.
Concern about the safety of young performers is nothing new, and the country actually passed a range of laws in 2014 aimed at protecting their rights and limiting their work hours.

However, in November of this year, investigators from The New York Times reported that members of the group NewJeans had signed contracts with record label Ador when they were aged 14 to 17 that effectively waived their rights to "sleep, rest and free choice."
The report also raised concerns about the members being required to cover a portion of the expenses for their training, as well as cosmetic surgery and dermatological treatments.
Ador is owned by Hybe, which represents BTS. Hybe told The New York Times in a statement that the company follows child-protection laws, and works hard to protect its entertainers.
However, the investigation also revealed that the contracts signed by NewJeans were missing standard child protection language.

NewJeans actually tried to leave Ador in November 2024. But almost a year later, the Seoul Central District Court declared that they still had to honor their contracts, which expire in 2029. Soon after, one of the five members was fired and sued for 33 billion won — about $25 million.
